description: Tertöns are treasure revealers of Tibetan Buddhism: visionary lamas and yogins who discover hidden terma, teachings concealed by Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal in caves, lakes, rocks, and monasteries. Entering meditative states, they often break convention to retrieve the hidden dharma. The terma system let Buddhist teachings evolve across centuries.
research_notes: Verified against the standard Wikipedia Tertön article and general scholarship on the terma tradition. The figure is a historical-institutional role rather than a single mythic being; description folds in input appearance (visionary lamas holding terma objects), behavior (meditative revelation), habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Tol(y)k is the paramount sea spirit of the Nivkh of Sakhalin and the Sea of Okhotsk coast, appearing as a sea serpent or whale with scales shimmering like dark water, or as a towering humanoid rising from the sea. Mercurial and powerful, it controls the sea's bounty—generous when respected, capsizing boats when angered. Its cult reflects the centrality of sea-mammal hunting to Nivkh life.
source: Nivkh indigenous religion — sea spirits of Sakhalin (scholarly and ethnographic surveys)
research_notes: Attested in ethnographic literature on Nivkh religion. Input provides appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance which are folded into the prose verbatim in content; no independent dedicated encyclopedia article was available, so source quality kept at good rather than expert.

description: Alpamysh Batyr is the central hero of the Kazakh version of the Alpamysh epic, a mighty batyr in traditional warrior attire who rides his magical horse Baychibar. Defender of his people, loyal husband, and wise leader, he represents the ideals of Turkic warrior culture. Recorded versions reach some 14,000 verses, performed by bakhshi singers to dombra accompaniment.
research_notes: The Alpamysh epic is a documented Turkic epic shared across Central Asia; input records early-20th-century folklorist recordings. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Aldar Qose is the beloved trickster of Kazakh folklore, a poor wanderer in threadbare clothing whose unassuming look hides a sharp mind. Never resorting to violence, he relies on elaborate verbal tricks to outsmart the wealthy and powerful, exposing greed and hypocrisy. His tales are social satire championing wit over wealth and power across the Kazakh steppe.
research_notes: Attested in Kazakh folklore; input cites e-history.kz and the J1110 clever-tricks motif. Description folds in input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Ak-Kula is the magical white stallion of Manas, greatest hero of the Kyrgyz epic, a white horse whose coat glows like moonlight and whose eyes betray human understanding. Born from the sea, it speaks with a human voice, giving prophetic warnings and fighting beside him, untameable by the unworthy. It is as iconic as Manas, embodying the bond between heroes and steeds.
research_notes: The speaking, prophetic steed of Manas is attested across versions of the Manas epic (B41/B211 motifs). Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Ay-Chürök ('Moon Swan') is a swan maiden of the Kyrgyz epic, the fairy wife of Semetey in the Manas cycle. As a human she is stunningly beautiful and luminous; as a swan, pure white and graceful, able to fly between human and celestial realms. Loyal and wise, she links the human and spirit worlds, a swan-maiden motif common across Central Asian folklore.
source: Kyrgyz oral tradition; Epic of Manas
research_notes: The Ay-Chürök swan-maiden figure is attested in the Manas cycle (D361 transformation motif). Description folds in the input appearance, shapeshifting behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Alpamysh (Alpomish) is the national heroic epic of Uzbekistan and its hero, a mighty warrior of the Kongrat tribe who rides the magical horse Baychibar. He defends his people against usurpers, fights for justice, and restores order to a divided tribe. The Uzbek version recorded from bard Fazil Yuldash-oghli exceeds 14,000 verses, performed by bakhshi singers.
research_notes: The Uzbek Alpomish is a documented national epic, a regional variant of the shared Turkic Alpamysh cycle. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Agaýunus Peri is a supernatural fairy-woman of the Turkmen epic, wife of the legendary hero Göroglu, a woman of luminous beauty in ethereal clothing who can appear and disappear at will, moving between human and spirit worlds. Loving and graceful, she reflects the Turkmen belief in peris as intermediaries between mortals and the unseen.
source: Epic of Göroglu; UNESCO ICH documentation
research_notes: The peri-fairy motif (F200) and Agaýunus as Göroglu's wife are attested in the Turkmen oral epic tradition. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: The Akhal-Teke horse spirit embodies Turkmenistan's national horse, a breed some 3,000 years old: metallic golden coat, serpentine neck, lean build. Traditionally spiritually bonded to its rider, it can cross 300 miles of Karakum Desert without water, guided by ancestral spirits, and is treated as a family member. Chinese records called them 'Heavenly Horses' said to 'sweat blood' from thin skin.
research_notes: The Akhal-Teke breed and its cultural halo are thoroughly documented (national symbol, 'Heavenly Horse' in Chinese sources). The 'spirit' framing is the input's mythological lens over a real, revered animal; description stays faithful to documented lore.

description: The argamak is the winged steed of Altai epic tradition, a magnificent white horse swift as the wind with glowing eyes and powerful wings. A loyal companion rather than mere transport, it travels between the three cosmic worlds, carrying heroes to the sky court of Bai-Ülgen and down to Erlik's underworld while advising and protecting its master.
research_notes: The flying/mythical steed (B41 motif) is attested across Altaian heroic epics, closely related to the Turkic tulpar. Description folds in the input appearance, inter-world behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Ak-Kaan, the White Khan, is a divine hero of Altai tradition, his body shining with divine radiance, wearing white robes and riding an argamak winged steed. He seeks truth and justice, defeats dark shamans and demons, and establishes a new faith blending shamanism with Buddhist and Tibetan influences—read as the mythological reflection of the Altai shift toward Burkhanism (Ak Jang) around 1900.
source: Altai oral tradition; folklore archives; Burkhanism (Ak Jang) studies
research_notes: The 'White Khan' figure is attested within the Ak Jang/Burkhanism religious reform movement of the Altai (Ak-Burkhan, white-banner faith), though the exact epic figure 'Ak-Kaan' lacks a single canonical scholarly article. Research found the Ak-Burkhan/Ak Jang context as the closest documented referent; description notes the identification transparently.

description: Abram Moos Kara Taaci is a powerful female shamanic figure of Altai epic tradition, linked to the underworld and called a daughter of Erlik. Capable of shapeshifting and wielding dark magic, she knows the lower world deeply and acts as both guide and challenger to epic heroes; in the Maadai-Kara epic she confronts Kögüdei Mergen. Her role reflects female shamanic power in Altai epic.
research_notes: Attested within Altai epic scholarship via the Maadai-Kara cycle (per input and prior-session verification). Some spellings and roles vary across tellings; description follows the input's own cultural data.

description: Abaasy are the malevolent lower-world spirits of Yakut (Sakha) cosmology: grotesque multi-headed monsters with iron teeth, bodies blending human and animal traits, some one-eyed or one-limbed. Sadistic and destructive, they bring disease, death, and misfortune, steal souls, and devour humans, and can only be defeated temporarily. Their eternal conflict with the Aiyy drives the Olonkho epics.
research_notes: The abaasy are thoroughly documented in Yakut mythology and olonkho scholarship. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance verbatim in content.

description: Aiyy are the benevolent celestial deities of Yakut (Sakha) cosmology, radiant beings of light often pictured as majestic humanoid figures in white robes, though some appear as horses, eagles, or swans. Benevolent yet distant, they respond to prayers and sacrifice rather than intervening directly, guiding chosen heroes to preserve cosmic balance against the chaotic Abaasy.
research_notes: The aiyy pantheon is foundational in Yakut cosmology and documented in ethnographic and epic scholarship. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Abai Geser ('the Mighty') is the great hero of the Buryat Epic of Gesar, a mighty warrior in celestial armor who rides a magical horse and radiates divine power as a son of the sky gods. Brave, cunning, relentless, he battles ever-stronger demonic foes, from giant rats to sun-devouring monsters, using trickery and disguise. The Geser epic is shared across Tibet, Mongolia, and Buryatia.
research_notes: The Buryat Abai Geser is documented through the shared Geser epic tradition and Buryat scholarship (Atai Ulaan article details his enemy-lord Atai Ulaan). Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Atai Ulan is the leader of the eastern, malevolent Tenger sky-gods in Buryat tradition, lifelong antagonist of Abai Geser in the Epic of Gesar. A gigantic dark figure, his body parts retain monstrous power even in death: dismembered, his scattered remains spawn the demons that plague the world. In one account, disease-spirits from his impaled toe give the mythological origin of gout.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia 'Atai Ulaan' and the sacred-texts 'Gesir Bogdo III' episode (dispute with Khan Tyurmas Tengeri). Details of disease-spirits and gout origin, his daughter Gaguurai Nogoon's marriage to Geser, and the sons Sagaan/Shara/Hara Hasar Buhe all confirmed.

description: Angara is the personified river spirit of Buryat folklore, a beautiful maiden whose flowing hair becomes the river's current and whose robes are woven of blue-green water, moving swiftly forward without looking back. Determined and rebellious, she defies her father, the lake spirit Baikal, for love; her escape represents the unstoppable force of the river flowing from Baikal to the Yenisei.
source: Buryat folklore — the Angara River spirit (regional collections)
research_notes: The Angara maiden legend (daughter of Baikal who fled to the Yenisei) is a well-known regional tale. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Anghir is a giant water bird of Buryat creation mythology, an immense diving bird able to reach the depths of the primordial ocean. As the obedient servant of the creator god, it ventures bravely into the unknown and brings up the first earth, the act through which the world and humanity come into being. Anghir is the Buryat Earth-Diver figure found across Siberian and Central Asian traditions.
research_notes: The Buryat earth-diver water bird is documented in creation-myth collections; the input cites the Handy Mythology Answer Book. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: The Amur tiger spirit, called Amba, is the most sacred animal in Nanai tradition, appearing as a giant Amur (Siberian) tiger with luminous eyes and glowing stripes that can stand on its hind legs and speak, sometimes as a tiger-human hybrid. Noble and powerful, it protects the forest and enforces natural law, rewarding respect for nature and punishing poachers and desecrators.
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia Nanai people article, which records great reverence for the tiger (Amba) and the bear (Doonta). Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Almas is the wildman or ape-man of Mongolian legend, reported chiefly from the western aimags and the Altai. It is described as a large man-like biped of five to six and a half feet, covered in thick dark brown, reddish, yellowish, or black hair except on hands and face, often with a heavy beard. Shy and reclusive, it is treated both as legend and as a possibly real primate.
source: digitalcollections.sit.edu — N. Wenzel, 'The Legend of the Almas: A Comparative and Critical Analysis'
research_notes: Verified via Wenzel's comparative study (SIT digital collections). All physical details in the description come from that source. Whether almas is folklore, surviving hominid, or hoax remains debated; the description reflects that ambiguity without fabricating encounters.

description: Manas is the legendary hero who united the scattered Kyrgyz tribes and namesake of one of the world's longest epic poems. The Kyrgyz trilogy 'Manas, Semetey, Seytek,' inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List, tells of tribes united into one nation. Tellers of both sexes and all ages recite it, often after a prophetic dream, in near-trance performances that can run up to thirteen hours.
research_notes: Verified via UNESCO ICH inscription and the Wikipedia Epic of Manas article. The 13-hour recitals, trance-like calling, oral master-to-apprentice transmission, and social functions all confirmed from the UNESCO nomination text.

description: Mangus (Mangadhai) are the multi-headed chaos-monsters of Mongol epic tradition, gigantic ogre-like beings often bearing 15, 25, or even 100 heads, with iron bodies, fangs, and claws. They devour livestock and people and battle the epic heroes, yet their souls are hidden outside the body in an animal or object, making them nearly immortal until the hidden weakness is destroyed.
source: Mongol epic poetry; Epic of Geser scholarship
research_notes: The mangas/mangad multi-headed demon-ogres of Mongol epic (including the Geser cycle) are attested in scholarly literature on Mongol epic poetry; the external-soul motif (G321) is standard. Web verification was rate-limited this session, but the figure's attestation is well established in folklore scholarship.

description: Mandukhai Khatun, 'Mandukhai the Wise,' is the legendary warrior-queen of 15th-century Mongolia, a noble queen in traditional headdress and armor who wields twin swords while riding horseback. A warrior who led armies into battle and a wise counselor in statecraft, she fought to reunify the Mongol nation alongside Dayan Khan and remains a lasting symbol of female power.
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia Mandukhai Khatun article (Mandukhai Sechen Khongorjin, reunification with Dayan Khan). Input's detail of leading troops while pregnant appears in popular accounts; description keeps the core documented biography.

description: Maadai-Kara is the eponymous elder hero of one of the greatest Altai heroic epics, a poem of 7,738 verses, shown in warrior clothing on an argamak winged horse. When Maadai-Kara and his wife are carried off to the underworld by Erlik, their son Kögüdei Mergen, the Heavenly Archer, journeys through all three cosmic worlds to rescue them. The epic was preserved by bard Elbek Kalkin.
research_notes: Verified via the Cambridge repository (Pegg) documenting the 2002 Ongudai performance by eelü bard Elbek Kalkin, and a 2023 dergipark article on the hero's mythic journey. Description corrects the input's conflation: Kögüdei Mergen is the acting hero who rescues Maadai-Kara.

description: In Yakut (Sakha) tradition the mammoth is the Great Underground Bull, a massive creature with huge tusks, thick shaggy fur, and a body that shakes the earth underground. Solitary and reclusive, it avoids sunlight; when it dies its body causes geological upheaval, and it is linked to tremors and mysterious giant bones. It explains frozen mammoth carcasses emerging from thawing permafrost.
source: nauka-dialog.ru — E. Vasilyeva, 'Mammoth in Mythological Representations of Yakuts' (2021)
research_notes: Verified via the nauka-dialog 2021 article: mammoth remains underpin Yakut images of the water bull and cold bull, and mammoth ideas appear in abaasy hero imagery of olonkho. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and explanatory cultural significance.

description: Machik Lapdron (1055–1153) is the great Tibetan yogini and founder of the Chöd tradition, pictured as a peaceful woman with a slight smile, holding the drum (damaru) and bell, implements of the Chöd practice she founded. Fearless and compassionate, she taught cutting attachment to the self, transforming demonic forces through wisdom, not confrontation. Her Chöd lineage remains a living practice.
source: https://wisdomcompassion.org (J. Edou, 'Machig Labdran and the Foundations of Chod'); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machik_Labdr%C3%B6n
research_notes: Verified via Jerome Edou's foundational study of Machig Labdron and Chöd (incl. biography sources such as 'Transforming the Aggregates into an Offering of Food' and the anonymous Dolpo manuscript at Lang Gonpa). Historical personage; description stays within documented biography and hagiography.

description: Merger is the foundational epic hero of the Nanai people of the Amur River region, a powerful warrior-shaman in animal-decorated armor who can transform into tiger, bird, or fish. He combines martial prowess with shamanic magic, undertaking spirit journeys across multiple worlds to protect his people. His kind of hero is preserved in the Hezhen Yimakan tradition (UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding).
research_notes: Verified via the UNESCO Yimakan inscription (oral heroic narrative of the Hezhen/Chinese Nanai, transmitting justice, bravery, and kindness) and the iplmyths Nanai survey (Tungusic people of the Amur, Songhua, Ussuri rivers). Description folds in the input appearance and shapeshifting behavior.

description: Mangadhai are the monstrous giants of the Mongolian steppe, destructive ogre-beings of superhuman strength and size who oppose the epic heroes. In tradition they can be countered through wit, strategic traps, and elders' knowledge. Mangadhai is essentially the same figure as the multi-headed mangas of Mongol epic (see mangus-mongol), sharing its hidden, external vulnerability.
research_notes: Mangadhai is a variant name for the mangas/mangad ogre-demons of Mongol epic poetry; the two input records describe the same figure. Attestation follows the same scholarship as mangus-mongol.

description: Ölgii-khorkhoi, the 'Mongolian Death Worm,' is the legendary cryptid of the Gobi Desert, a thick, fat worm, bright red or orange, as thick as a man's arm, eyeless and mouthless, sometimes with spikes. Buried in sand and emerging after rain, it is said to kill camels and humans with corrosive spit or electric discharge. Popularized in the West since Roy Chapman Andrews, it remains unconfirmed.
research_notes: The legend is attested as folklore/cryptozoology (popularized by Andrews in the 1920s and by Ivan Mackerle); the worm's existence is unconfirmed. Description reflects attested lore without asserting the creature is real. Input archetype 'water-spirit' is inaccurate — it is a desert serpent/cryptid; flagged.

description: The Lord of the Gobi is a desert spirit of southern Mongolia, described as a towering figure of sand and wind, sometimes a dust devil, that can also appear as an old man or a shimmering form in the heat haze. It tests desert travelers for hospitality and worthiness, rewarding the kind with safe passage and hidden water, punishing the cruel, embodying the harsh but just nature of the Gobi.
source: Mongolian oral tradition; Gobi folklore collections; tellstory.net — 'The White Old Man of the West'
research_notes: The exact title 'Lord of the Gobi' was not found in standard reference works; the closest documented figure is Tsagaan Övgön (White Old Man of the West), a spirit who blesses homes, herds, and travelers and rewards hospitality and one's word. Sandstorm-control specifics appear only in popularized retellings and are flagged as uncertain.

description: The loon, also called the golden or diving bird, is the creation bird of Altai mythology, small but infinitely courageous, diving into the infinite primordial ocean and risking its life to bring up the mud from which the earth is made. Central to the Altai creation account, the diving-bird motif connects Altaian tradition to the broader family of Siberian and circumpolar earth-diver cosmogonies.
research_notes: The Altai earth-diver loon/goldeneye (A810 motif) is documented in creation-myth collections, related to the Buryat Anghir figure. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Luus are the dragon-like water spirits of Buryat tradition, serpentine beings with water-shimmering scales, deer-like horns, and glowing green eyes, sometimes appearing as whirlpools or mist. Territorial and mercurial, they may be generous with fish or wrathful with storms, and must be approached with proper ritual. Their veneration reflects the importance of Lake Baikal and its watershed.
source: trad-culture.ru — L. Dampilova (Institute for Mongolian, Buddhist and Tibetan Studies, RAS), on Luus/Luz spirits
research_notes: Verified via Dampilova's article: Luz/Lusad are terrestrial and subterranean water-spirits, Luu are heavenly dragons, with common serpentine features and roles as divine helpers/protectors in ritual folklore. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Luus are water-serpent guardians of Mongolian folklore, with iridescent scales, sometimes horns or wings, guarding lakes, rivers, and sacred springs. Benevolent if respected, malevolent if their waters are polluted, they govern the land's fertility. The complex spans Luz/Lusad, terrestrial and subterranean water-spirits, and Luu, heavenly dragon helpers in ritual tradition.
source: trad-culture.ru — L. Dampilova (Institute for Mongolian, Buddhist and Tibetan Studies, RAS), on Luus/Luz spirits
research_notes: Same Luz/Lusad/Luu complex verified for Mongolian (and Buryat) contexts via Dampilova's article. Description folds in the input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure of Kyrgyz folklore. No source confirms a forest spirit named 'Yetga-chach,' described as an old hunter with a huge beard who protects game and trees; searches return only the unrelated Kyrgyz and Turkic word 'chach' (hair) and an unrelated Ukrainian forest deity. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.
research_notes: Searches (web) returned only dictionary entries for Kyrgyz/Uyghur 'çach/chach' = hair (speak.tatar, Uyghur-Kyrgyz dictionary) and the Ukrainian Chuhaister forest deity. No Kyrgyz-language or scholarly source for 'Yetga-chach' was found; likely a neologism or conflation. Marked unattested per policy; flagged for potential removal.

description: Yuch-Kurbustan is a supreme celestial deity of Altai cosmology, a being of pure light in the highest heavens, never shown in human form, only as divine radiance. It wields supreme authority, aids heroes, and judges gods and humans. Apex of the divine hierarchy in Altaian epic, it is invoked in the most sacred narratives—in the Maadai-Kara epic it aids Kögüdei Mergen against Erlik's forces.
research_notes: Yuch-Kurbustan relates to the Buryat/Mongol Khormusta (Kurbustan, ultimately Indra-derived) supreme-deity complex; attestation is via Altai epic tradition per input and prior-session verification. Specialized dedicated studies are limited, hence fair.
